title: Politics and public institutions
subtitle: monarchy, constituency, cast a vote, coalition
summary: Name types of government, describe how presidential and parliamentary systems work, and talk about elections - candidates, constituencies, ballot papers and majorities.

lesson.heading: Types of government
rows: a state governed by representatives and, usually, a president (e.g. USA, France)
a state ruled by a king or queen (e.g. UK, Sweden)
a union of political units such as provinces under a central government (e.g. USA)
government of, by and for the people
a system of government run by a dictator

lesson.heading: Presidential government
lesson.text: In the United States the powers of the **President** and the **legislature** (Congress) are separate, and the two branches are **elected** separately. The President is elected for a four-year **term**.

examples.text: The President can **appoint** or **nominate** high officials, including **cabinet members** and federal judges.
examples.note: appoint = decide who to give a position of authority to

examples.text: The President leads a major party, usually the **majority party** in Congress.
examples.note: the majority party = the political party which won the most votes

examples.text: Congress consists of two houses, the **House of Representatives** and the **Senate**.

lesson.heading: Parliamentary government
lesson.text: In the United Kingdom the government consists of a **legislature** (Parliament) and a **Cabinet of Ministers** from the majority party. The **Prime Minister** is the head of the government and **heads** the Cabinet.

examples.text: If no party has an overall **majority**, there may be a **coalition government** formed from more than one party.
Parliament consists of two **chambers**, the House of Commons and the House of Lords.
**MPs** are members of parliament elected from each **constituency** to the House of Commons.
examples.note: a constituency is a geographical voting area

lesson.heading: Parliamentary elections
lesson.text: During a **general election** each constituency chooses which politician it wants as its representative. There are usually several **candidates**, who are all **standing** (or **running**) for Parliament and present their party's **policies**, i.e. its plans.

examples.text: On **polling day** every adult goes to the **polling station**.
You **cast a vote** by marking a cross on your **ballot paper**.
The candidate who gets the **majority** of votes **wins the seat**.
If the vote is very close, the constituency may be called a **marginal seat**.

lesson.heading: Word families
rows: elector; electorate (the group of people entitled to vote)

lesson.text: Politics is the activity and politician is the person, but a party's plans are its policy - never ~~its politics~~ when you mean its plans.

exercises.prompt: A member of parliament ___ his or her constituency.
exercises.explanation: An MP acts officially for the people of a constituency, so he or she represents it.

exercises.prompt: India gained ___ from the UK in 1948.
exercises.explanation: Independence is freedom from outside control.

exercises.prompt: On ___ day electors cast their votes.
exercises.explanation: Polling day is the day of the election; you vote at a polling station.

exercises.prompt: She's ___ for Parliament in the next election.
exercises.explanation: Candidates stand or run for Parliament.

exercises.prompt: His father was ___ MP for Cambridge City.
exercises.explanation: People are elected to a seat by vote.
A policy is a plan of action; politics is the activity in general.

exercises.prompt: The USA is a ___ of 50 states.
exercises.explanation: A federation is a union of political units under a central government.

exercises.prompt: Although modern monarchs are said to ___ over their countries, they have little real power.
exercises.explanation: A king or queen rules; the elected government governs.

exercises.prompt: Parliament in the UK consists of two ___: the House of Commons and the House of Lords.
exercises.explanation: The two chambers of Parliament are the Commons and the Lords.

exercises.prompt: The country is divided into ___, each of which elects an MP to the House of Commons.
exercises.explanation: A constituency is a geographical voting area.

exercises.prompt: The ruling party in the Commons is the one which gains a ___ of seats.
exercises.explanation: The majority party is the one that won the most votes.

exercises.prompt: Sometimes more than one party may share power in a ___ government.
exercises.explanation: A coalition government is formed from more than one party.

exercises.prompt: The Prime Minister may call a general ___ at any time within the five-year period.
exercises.explanation: A general election is when the whole country votes for a new Parliament.
